reading.body:
Nonprofit AI adoption is measured by sector research organizations, not a real-time registry, and the binding constraint is governance capacity rather than compute or power.

The seven sources split the problem into distinct angles. CEP and NTEN survey how foundations and nonprofits use AI for operations, program delivery, and communications. The AI Equity Project tracks access and training gaps. Candid tracks grantmaking for AI adoption and technology infrastructure. Census BTOS includes nonprofit-heavy service sectors in its adoption series, and Stanford HAI reports macro social impact. No single entity maintains a real-time registry.

The practical uses named are grant writing, donor analytics, and service delivery on small budgets. Because governance capacity is the stated constraint, AI scaling in this sector is limited by oversight and policy adoption, not by access to compute or grid power. The data does not support a compute or power constraint for nonprofits.

The data does not provide adoption rates, budget figures, or compute and power requirements. It identifies who publishes sector research, not how many nonprofits have deployed AI or what infrastructure they use.

summary: Grant writing, donor analytics, and service delivery are the practical uses; governance capacity is the constraint. No single entity keeps a real-time registry of nonprofit AI adoption - coverage comes from sector research organizations, and this page names the ones that actually publish it.

analysis.body:
The Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey, which covers other services under NAICS 81, including grantmaking and civic organizations, puts AI use at 15.0% of firms in the latest period, up from 13.7% in the prior period. The survey asks whether the business used AI in the last two weeks, and the Census Bureau notes that some values in the series are suppressed. That is the only measured adoption figure in the material here, and it applies to a sector grouping broader than nonprofits alone.

The sources describe what the sector does with the technology in general terms rather than with measured deployment detail. The Center for Effective Philanthropy examines how foundations and nonprofits use AI for operations, program delivery, and communications. NTEN runs regular sector-wide research on technology investment, digital maturity, and AI policy adoption among nonprofits, and frames nonprofit technology as marked by inequities within organizations and across the sector that it says must be dismantled. The AI Equity Project works on accessibility and training, building structured learning pathways and intergenerational programs, turning public libraries and community spaces into learning environments where senior citizens and student volunteers explore practical AI tools, and providing standardized technical curricula to underrepresented communities.

On the funding side, Candid, the nonprofit data organization behind GuideStar and Foundation Center, tracks grantmaking trends including funding directed toward AI adoption and technology infrastructure. Candid's page emphasizes that most grant funding, and sometimes donations, come with strings attached, and that most people do not see the heavy burden this places on nonprofits. It also notes that recognition, media coverage, partnerships, and growth do not guarantee a nonprofit's financial sustainability, and that continued unrestricted support is needed. The World of AI's own catalogue of nonprofits and open source foundations lists four individually verified organizations, two nonprofits and two open-source foundations, and states plainly that none are infrastructure builders in the compute-or-power sense. It describes LMSYS as stewarding Chatbot Arena, a shared evaluation platform used to benchmark model quality, Khan Academy as an end-user of AI in education rather than a producer of it, and the Krita Foundation and Blender Foundation as stewards of creative software that AI-generated imagery and 3D content increasingly intersect with. The same page states what it does not cover: no training compute providers, no standards bodies setting grid or data-center specifications, and no open-model foundations releasing weights, with the notes confirming only organizational structure and nonprofit status, not funding scale, compute access, or governance detail.

The material does not report ROI figures for nonprofit AI deployment, and it does not report dollar amounts or adoption rates for specific tools. Stanford HAI's AI Index is listed as the citable macro series on AI's social impact and implementation across mission-driven and public-sector organizations, but no findings from it appear in these excerpts. Where the sources are silent on returns, cost savings, or grant funding totals, there is nothing here to cite.

The regulatory posture is also largely absent from this material. NTEN's page points to AI policy adoption as a subject of its research, and the World of AI page notes that its wider site tracks state AI laws and a lawsuit tracker, but no specific rule, requirement, or compliance obligation for nonprofits appears in these excerpts. The recurring theme the sources do state is capacity: Candid describes restricted funding as a heavy burden, NTEN describes inequities in technology use and funding, and the AI Equity Project describes an access and training gap across community organizations.

For a reader deciding whether to deploy, the material supports a narrow set of takeaways. Measured adoption in the Census Bureau's other services grouping is 15.0%, so most firms in that grouping are not using AI in any given two-week window. The named uses in these sources are operational and programmatic, including operations, program delivery, and communications per the Center for Effective Philanthropy, and the constraints the sources emphasize are money and skills rather than technology availability. Candid's point about restricted funding and NTEN's point about equity in technology investment suggest that budget flexibility and staff capability, not tool access alone, are where the sector's sources locate the difficulty.

https://cep.org/.brief: The page from the Center for Effective Philanthropy features an article by Kevin Bolduc, who is identified as vice president of assessment and advisory services. The article’s title asks how one collaborative’s movement-led participatory model makes a difference for grantees. The harvested text does not include any further details or findings.

https://candid.org/.brief: Candid describes itself as a provider of grants and nonprofit data intended to help people find funding, research nonprofits and connect with funders. It says analysts, advocates and philanthropists use its information to build a broad picture of social sector activity, and it invites readers to learn how it collects, organises and distributes that data. The page also flags several topics it covers: the conditions attached to most grant funding and some donations, and the strain those conditions place on nonprofits; one foundation's stated reasons for sharing its grantmaking data with Candid, which it frames as a matter of transparency; and the argument that recognition, media coverage, partnerships and growth do not by themselves make a nonprofit financially sustainable, since it needs ongoing unrestricted support. It notes that impact evaluations are growing in importance for nonprofits and funders alike, and offers an email list for insights, trends, product updates and research.

https://www.nten.org/.brief: NTEN presents itself as a nonprofit community focused on using technology for social change. It offers networking opportunities, job listings, and professional development resources such as certificates and scholarships. Members can pledge to use an Equity Guide and support open-source developers. NTEN also encourages participation in committees on accessibility, equity, and programs.

https://theaiequityproject.org/.brief: The AI Equity Project reports that it develops structured educational routes and cross-generational initiatives aimed at making AI usable, ethical, and practical for every community. It says it converts public libraries and local community venues into hands-on learning settings where older adults and student volunteers jointly try out practical AI tools. The organization also describes a worldwide network that supplies standardized technical curricula and training materials to underrepresented groups, with support structures meant to ensure each student directly helps deploy machine learning architectures. Its International AI for Impact Challenge asks engineering candidates to propose operational algorithms for real-world issues, and top entrants receive engineering lab partnerships, academic research access, and intellectual property advice.

https://theworldofai.org/ai-ecosystem/ec.brief: The page catalogues four verified organisations ,  two nonprofits and two open-source foundations ,  whose work touches AI tooling and evaluation, though the page states none of them build compute or power infrastructure. It describes LMSYS as the most directly AI-focused entry, stewarding the Chatbot Arena evaluation platform used by the wider AI community to benchmark model quality, and notes that such neutral evaluation sits outside the commercial interests of the labs being assessed. Khan Academy is characterised as an end user rather than a producer of AI in education, while the Krita Foundation and Blender Foundation steward creative software whose missions predate AI even as AI-generated imagery and 3D content increasingly intersect with it. The page states its own limits plainly: it lists no training compute providers, no standards bodies for grid or data-centre specifications, and no open-model foundations releasing weights publicly, and its notes confirm only organisational structure and nonprofit status rather than funding scale, compute access or governance detail.
